title: Selective Question Answering under Domain Shift
research_question: Can selective question answering remain reliable under an unknown domain shift by learning a confidence calibrator from source-domain examples and examples from a different known out-of-domain dataset?
methodology: A BERT-base question-answering model is trained on SQuAD, while a separate random-forest calibrator predicts whether the QA model's answer will be correct. The calibrator uses passage length, predicted-answer length, and the top five answer probabilities, and is trained on a mixture of source-domain examples and labeled examples from one known out-of-domain dataset. Evaluation mixes SQuAD with a different, previously unseen out-of-domain dataset and averages results across ordered choices drawn from five QA datasets; baselines include maximum softmax probability, a source-only calibrator, QA retraining with known out-of-domain data, test-time dropout, and an outlier detector.

key_findings.finding: Training the calibrator with source and known out-of-domain data raised average coverage at 80% target accuracy to about 56.1%, compared with 48.2% for maximum softmax probability.

Using known out-of-domain data to train the confidence calibrator was more effective for selective QA than merely retraining the QA model with that data, reaching about 56.1% versus 51.8% coverage at 80% target accuracy.

A calibrator trained on both source and known out-of-domain examples also outperformed a source-only calibrator at the same target accuracy, demonstrating transfer of calibration information across domains.
Adding test-time dropout-derived features improved the calibrator further, reaching about 60.0% coverage at 80% target accuracy, but required repeated inference passes.
Maximum softmax probability is systematically overconfident on shifted domains, whereas the learned calibrator narrows the confidence-quality gap between source and out-of-domain examples.
key_findings.section: Analysis of calibration under domain shift

key_findings.finding: A generic outlier detector was substantially weaker for selective QA than directly learning to predict answer correctness.

limitations: The approach assumes access to labeled examples from a known out-of-domain distribution, which may not exist or may not resemble the future unknown domain.
Experiments center on extractive question answering with a SQuAD-trained BERT-base model and do not establish behavior for free-form long-form generation.
The evaluation uses an offline mixture of source and shifted datasets rather than a temporally evolving online stream.
The learned feature relationships may themselves be domain dependent; simple properties such as question or passage length can behave differently across datasets.
Test-time dropout improves selective performance but incurs substantial inference overhead because many stochastic forward passes are required.
The method provides empirical risk-coverage performance rather than a finite-sample statistical guarantee that a specified risk constraint will hold.
The study does not evaluate evidence completeness, partial support within compound claims, superseded work-item states, or longitudinal omission.
raw_claims: The QA model is trained on SQuAD and evaluated under mixtures containing a previously unseen question-answering domain.
The calibrator estimates the probability that the underlying QA model's answer is correct.
Its features include passage length, predicted-answer length, and the five largest answer probabilities.
The experiments rotate among TriviaQA, HotpotQA, NewsQA, Natural Questions, and SearchQA as shifted domains.
The source-plus-known-domain calibrator achieves higher selective coverage than maximum answer probability at fixed target accuracy.
Known out-of-domain data remains useful even when it comes from a different domain than the unknown test shift.
Test-time dropout improves the reported risk-coverage results but requires repeated model evaluations.
An outlier detector that focuses on domain membership performs worse than a calibrator trained to predict answer correctness.
The authors release code, data, and experiment artifacts through CodaLab.
